path.title: SOC Analyst Learning Path
path.description: A safe, step-by-step foundation for understanding computers, operating systems, networks, and defensive security operations.

modules.title: Computer Fundamentals
modules.description: Learn what a computer does and how its parts work together before studying networks or security.

topics.title: What is a computer?
topics.definition: A computer is an electronic device that follows instructions to receive, work with, store, and share information.
topics.explanation: A computer does not understand a task the way a person does. Software gives it instructions. The computer represents information as tiny on-or-off values called bits, then combines those values to work with text, pictures, sound, and numbers. A phone, laptop, server, and smart television are all computers, even though they look different.
topics.importance: A SOC Analyst reviews information created by computers. Knowing that devices follow instructions helps you ask which device, account, program, or event produced a record.
steps: A person or another device supplies input.
A program gives the computer instructions for that input.
The processor and memory help perform the instructions.
The computer displays, sends, or stores the result.
topics.example: When you type a document, the keyboard supplies letters, the writing program arranges them, and the screen shows the document. Saving stores a copy so it can be opened later.
topics.cyberExample: A login attempt is an input to a computer service. The service checks its rules and produces a result, such as a successful or failed login record. A defender reads that record to understand what happened.

terms.meaning: Information or a signal given to a computer.
A step that tells software or hardware what operation to perform.
The smallest basic unit of computer data, represented as 0 or 1.

topics.diagram:
INPUT  ->  INSTRUCTIONS AND PROCESSING  ->  OUTPUT
                         |                 |
                         +---- STORAGE ----+
topics.activity: Name one input, one action, and one output when you search for a file on your own device. Do not open files that you do not recognize.

topics.title: Hardware and software
topics.definition: Hardware is the physical equipment in a computer. Software is the set of programs and instructions that tell the equipment what to do.
topics.explanation: A screen, keyboard, processor, and storage drive are hardware because you can physically touch them. An operating system, browser, and document editor are software. The two depend on each other: software needs hardware to run, and hardware needs instructions to perform useful work. Firmware is a small kind of software stored in a device to help it start or control basic functions.
topics.importance: Security problems can involve either side. A damaged drive is a hardware issue; an outdated browser is a software issue. Analysts should describe which component is involved instead of calling every problem a computer virus.
steps: The device starts using built-in startup instructions.
The operating system loads from storage into memory.
A person opens an application.
The application asks the operating system to use hardware such as the screen, network, or storage.
topics.example: A laptop's camera is hardware. A video meeting application is software. The operating system controls access so the application can use the camera when allowed.
topics.cyberExample: A security update changes software to correct a weakness. A physical security lock protects hardware from being removed. Both can help protect the same laptop.

terms.meaning: Physical computer parts and connected devices.
Programs and instructions executed by a computer.
Low-level software stored on a device to control basic operation.

topics.diagram:
PERSON -> APPLICATION -> OPERATING SYSTEM -> HARDWARE
                         software                 physical parts
topics.activity: Choose three items near you and label each as hardware or software. For a software item, name the hardware it needs to work.

lessons.title: 1.2 The parts that do the work

topics.title: CPU, RAM, and storage
topics.definition: The CPU performs instructions, RAM holds information the computer is using right now, and storage keeps information for later.
topics.explanation: The CPU, or central processing unit, reads and carries out program instructions. RAM, or random-access memory, is fast temporary workspace. Its contents usually disappear when power is removed. Storage, such as an SSD or hard drive, keeps files and programs after shutdown. These parts have different jobs; adding storage does not automatically make a processor faster.
topics.importance: SOC tools and computers need enough memory and storage to process and retain logs. Understanding the difference helps an analyst describe a full disk, a busy processor, or limited memory accurately.
steps: A program is saved on storage.
When opened, needed instructions and data are copied into RAM.
The CPU works on those instructions and data.
The results can be displayed or saved back to storage.
topics.example: A recipe book on a shelf is like storage. The page you are currently using is like RAM. The person following each instruction is like the CPU.
topics.cyberExample: If a device is lost, information saved on its storage may be exposed unless suitable protections, such as full-disk encryption and a strong sign-in, were enabled. Those controls reduce risk but do not replace backups or account security.

terms.meaning: The processor that carries out program instructions.
Fast, temporary working memory used while programs run.
Devices that keep files and programs when power is off.
A method that makes data unreadable without the required key.

topics.diagram:
STORAGE (keeps files) -> RAM (current work) <-> CPU (does instructions)
                                  results can be saved back to storage
topics.activity: Open a file manager and note the names of one storage device and one file. Do not change or delete anything.

topics.title: Input and output devices
topics.definition: An input device sends information to a computer. An output device presents information from the computer.
topics.explanation: A keyboard, mouse, microphone, and camera can provide input. A screen, speaker, and printer can provide output. Some devices do both: a touch screen displays information and detects taps. Data can also enter or leave through a network connection or removable storage.
topics.importance: Knowing how information enters and leaves a device helps with safe handling. A file can arrive through email, a download, a USB drive, or a network service, and each path may need different checks.
steps: A person or connected device creates a signal.
An input component passes the signal to an application or operating system.
The computer processes it.
An output component displays, plays, prints, or sends the result.
topics.example: A microphone turns sound into digital information. A meeting application sends it to other participants and plays their audio through speakers.
topics.cyberExample: An unexpected USB drive is an untrusted input source. Follow your organization's policy and do not connect unknown devices to work equipment.

terms.meaning: A device connected to a computer, such as a keyboard or printer.
Portable storage such as a USB drive.
A connection point through which devices or programs exchange information.

topics.diagram: KEYBOARD / CAMERA / NETWORK -> COMPUTER -> SCREEN / SPEAKER / NETWORK
topics.activity: Draw a small input-process-output diagram for taking a photo with a phone. Mark where the image is stored.

topics.title: Operating systems
topics.definition: An operating system is the main software that manages a computer's hardware and provides common services to applications.
topics.explanation: Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, and iOS are operating systems. The operating system starts the device, manages memory and files, runs programs, and coordinates devices. It also provides accounts and permissions so different people and applications do not automatically receive the same access.
topics.importance: Security analysts need to know which operating system produced an event because log locations, account names, tools, and security settings differ between systems.
steps: Startup instructions locate the operating system.
The operating system loads and prepares the device.
A user signs in and opens an application.
The operating system manages the application's requests for files, memory, devices, and network access.
topics.example: When you print a document, the writing application asks the operating system to send it to the selected printer.
topics.cyberExample: Operating-system updates can correct security weaknesses. Organizations test and apply updates through a managed process so devices remain supported and protected.

terms.meaning: Software designed to help a person perform a task.
A named identity used to access a device or service.
A rule describing which actions an account or program may perform.

topics.diagram: USER -> APPLICATION -> OPERATING SYSTEM -> CPU, MEMORY, FILES, DEVICES
topics.activity: Find the operating-system name and version on your device using its normal settings screen. Do not install or change anything.

topics.title: Files, folders, and processes
topics.definition: A file is a named collection of information, a folder organizes files, and a process is a program that is currently running.
topics.explanation: Documents, pictures, and logs are commonly stored as files. Folders help people organize them in a hierarchy. A path describes where an item is located. A process is an active instance of a program; one application may create more than one process. A filename extension can suggest a file type, but it does not prove that the file is safe.
topics.importance: SOC Analysts often investigate file paths, application names, and process records. These details help distinguish expected activity from activity that needs more review.
steps: A program or person creates or opens a file.
The operating system checks the file path and access permissions.
When a program starts, the operating system creates a process.
The process reads or writes permitted data and ends when its work is complete.
topics.example: A photo may be stored at a path such as Pictures/Trip/photo.jpg. Opening it starts a photo-viewing process.
topics.cyberExample: A log may record that a process opened a file at an unusual time. That is a clue for an analyst, not proof by itself; the account, device, and surrounding events also matter.

terms.meaning: The location of a file or folder in a storage hierarchy.
The ending of a filename that often indicates its format, such as .txt.
A running instance of a program.
A time-ordered record of events.

topics.diagram:
STORAGE
  +-- Documents
  |     +-- notes.txt
  +-- Pictures
        +-- photo.jpg  -> open -> photo-viewer process
topics.activity: Create a new empty folder in your personal practice area, give it a clear name, and then remove it using the normal file manager if you no longer need it.

topics.title: How computer work fits together
topics.definition: A computer completes a task by coordinating input, software instructions, processing, memory, storage, and output.
topics.explanation: The parts work together rather than acting alone. A program requests an operation from the operating system. The operating system coordinates access to the processor, memory, storage, and connected devices. Some tasks also send information across a network. The exact details differ by device, but the basic flow is similar.
topics.importance: This model helps analysts trace an event. You can ask what started the activity, which program handled it, what resource it used, and where the result went.
steps: A person, timer, or device starts an action.
An application asks the operating system to perform work.
The CPU processes instructions using information in memory.
The application displays a result or asks the system to store or send it.
topics.example: A calendar reminder starts at a chosen time, the calendar application reads the reminder, and the operating system displays a notification.
topics.cyberExample: A sign-in service receives a login attempt, checks account rules, and records the outcome. An analyst can use the record's time and device context to investigate an unusual sign-in.

terms.meaning: A part of a computer used by a task, such as memory, storage, or a network connection.
Something that happened and may be recorded by a system.
Related details that help explain an event.

topics.diagram:
ACTION -> APPLICATION -> OPERATING SYSTEM -> PROCESSOR / MEMORY
                                      |                    |
                                      +-- STORAGE / NETWORK / OUTPUT
topics.activity: Pick a normal task, such as saving a note. Write down its starting action, the application, and where the result is stored.

topics.title: Basic computer terminology
topics.definition: Computer terminology is a shared set of words for describing devices, programs, information, and actions precisely.
topics.explanation: A device is a piece of equipment. A user is a person or service identity that uses a device. Data is information a computer can store or process. A network connects devices so they can exchange data. A server is a computer or program that provides a service to other computers, called clients. These words describe roles and functions, not necessarily different kinds of physical boxes.
topics.importance: Clear terms reduce confusion when writing notes or handing an investigation to another analyst. For example, saying which server and account were involved is more useful than writing only that 'the system acted strangely.'
steps: Name the device or service involved.
Identify the account or program that acted.
Describe the data or resource involved.
Record what happened and when, using observed facts.
topics.example: A laptop (device) uses a browser (program) under a learner account (user) to request a page from a web server (service).
topics.cyberExample: An incident note might say: 'The test workstation recorded a failed sign-in for the training account at 10:14.' This names the device, event, account, and time without guessing why it happened.

terms.meaning: A device or program that requests a service.
A device or program that provides a service.
Information that can be stored, processed, or sent.
A person or service identity acting on a computer.

topics.diagram: CLIENT (requests)  <---- network ---->  SERVER (provides a service)
topics.activity: Rewrite 'the computer did something odd' as a factual note using a device, program or account, observed event, and time. Use fictional details.

quiz.prompt: Which statement best describes a computer?
choices: A device that follows instructions to work with information
A device that only stores pictures
quiz.explanation: Computers follow instructions to receive, process, store, and share information.

quiz.prompt: Which part usually keeps files when a computer is turned off?
quiz.explanation: Storage keeps files and programs when power is off; RAM is temporary working memory.

quiz.prompt: What is a process?
choices: A program that is currently running
quiz.explanation: A process is an active instance of a program.

quiz.prompt: What is the operating system's role?
choices: Manage hardware and provide services to applications
Guarantee that every file is safe
quiz.explanation: The operating system coordinates hardware, files, accounts, and application requests.

quiz.prompt: A file extension proves a file is safe. True or false?
quiz.explanation: An extension can suggest a format, but it does not prove that a file is safe.

modules.title: Networking Fundamentals
modules.description: Understand how devices address each other and exchange information across local and wide networks.

topics.title: What is a computer network?
topics.definition: A computer network is a group of connected devices that can exchange information using agreed rules.
topics.explanation: A connection may use a cable, radio signal, or another communication link. Devices use protocols, which are shared rules, to format and move information. A network can connect two devices in one room or many networks across countries. A network connection does not automatically mean every device can access every other device.
topics.importance: SOC Analysts review network records to understand which systems communicated, when they communicated, and whether that activity fits expected use.
steps: A device prepares information to send.
Network rules divide and label the information for delivery.
Network equipment moves it toward the destination.
The receiving device checks and uses the information according to its own rules.
topics.example: A laptop sends a request to a school file service over the school's local network. The service returns a file only if access is allowed.
topics.cyberExample: A firewall record may show a device attempting to contact a service. Analysts compare the source, destination, time, and business purpose before deciding whether to escalate.

terms.meaning: Agreed rules that allow devices to communicate.
Information moving across a network.
A device or service that sends or receives network traffic.

topics.diagram:
LAPTOP ---- local network equipment ---- FILE SERVICE
       shared rules describe how information is exchanged
topics.activity: Draw the devices used to connect your home or school to a website. Label which links are local and which leave the local network.

topics.title: LAN, WAN, and the internet
topics.definition: A LAN connects devices in a limited local area, a WAN connects networks over a larger area, and the internet is a worldwide network of networks.
topics.explanation: A home, office, or school may operate a local area network (LAN). A wide area network (WAN) connects locations that are far apart, often through a service provider. The internet connects many independently managed networks using common protocols. The Wi-Fi signal in a room is a local access method; Wi-Fi itself is not the internet.
topics.importance: Knowing the scope of a network helps determine where a device is and which team may own the equipment. It also helps explain why a local connection can work while an internet service is unavailable.
steps: A device connects to a nearby LAN using cable or Wi-Fi.
A router may forward traffic from the LAN toward another network.
Service-provider networks carry traffic over larger distances.
The destination network delivers information to the requested service.
topics.example: A student connects a laptop to a campus Wi-Fi network. The campus LAN then provides access to local printers and, through a router and provider, the internet.
topics.cyberExample: An organization may keep staff devices on a managed network while offering visitors a separate guest network. Separation limits unnecessary access between groups.

terms.meaning: Local area network covering a limited place.
Wide area network that connects distant networks.
A global collection of interconnected networks.
A wireless local networking technology.

topics.diagram: DEVICE -> LAN -> ROUTER -> PROVIDER NETWORKS -> INTERNET -> SERVICE
topics.activity: Classify three example connections as local or wide-area: a printer in the same room, a campus network, and a public website.

topics.title: IP addresses and MAC addresses
topics.definition: An IP address identifies a network endpoint for communication, while a MAC address identifies a network interface on its local network link.
topics.explanation: Internet Protocol (IP) addresses help route data between networks. A device may have different IP addresses on different networks, and a network can assign an address temporarily. A Media Access Control (MAC) address is used for local-link delivery by network technology such as Ethernet or Wi-Fi. It is not a reliable public identity for a person and may be randomized by modern devices.
topics.importance: Analysts may see IP addresses in logs and packet summaries. Understanding that addresses identify connections or interfaces, not people, prevents unsupported conclusions.
steps: An application identifies a service using a name or address.
The device uses an IP address to direct traffic toward a network destination.
On a local link, network equipment uses link-level information such as a MAC address.
Routers forward traffic between networks using IP information.
topics.example: A laptop can keep the same MAC address on its Wi-Fi interface while receiving a different local IP address at home and at school.
topics.cyberExample: A log entry containing an IP address is one clue. A defender should also consider the time, device, account, network assignment, and other records before attributing activity.

terms.meaning: A network-layer address used to identify a destination for routing.
A link-layer address used to deliver data on a local network segment.
A device component that connects to a network.

topics.diagram:
BETWEEN NETWORKS: IP address guides routing
ON A LOCAL LINK: MAC address helps deliver a frame
topics.activity: Use your device's normal network settings to observe whether it shows an IP address. Do not share the value publicly.

topics.title: Public and private IP addresses
topics.definition: A public IP address is globally routable on the internet. A private IP address is used inside private networks and is not directly routed across the public internet.
topics.explanation: Home and office devices commonly use private addresses behind a router. The router can translate between local addresses and a public address for many outgoing connections. Private address ranges are reused by many organizations, so a private address alone does not identify a unique device worldwide. Public addresses can also change over time.
topics.importance: This distinction helps SOC Analysts understand network logs and avoid treating a private address as a unique internet-wide identity.
steps: A device receives a private address on its local network.
It sends traffic to its local router.
The router forwards permitted traffic using an internet-facing address.
Return traffic is directed back through the router to the correct local device.
topics.example: Several laptops at home may have different private addresses but share one public address when visiting a website.
topics.cyberExample: Addresses in 192.0.2.0/24 and 203.0.113.0/24 are reserved for documentation examples. A training log using them is fictional and should not be treated as a real source.

terms.meaning: An address intended for use within a private network.
An address that can be routed across the public internet.
Network Address Translation; a method routers use to map addresses between networks.

topics.diagram: LAPTOP 192.168.x.x -> HOME ROUTER -> PUBLIC ADDRESS -> WEBSITE
topics.activity: Explain why two different homes may both use a private address beginning with 192.168. Do not probe or scan any network.

topics.title: DNS and DHCP
topics.definition: DNS helps translate service names into network information, while DHCP automatically provides network settings to devices.
topics.explanation: The Domain Name System (DNS) lets people use names such as example.org instead of memorizing numeric addresses. A DNS response can contain different kinds of records and may change. Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) commonly gives a device an IP address, router, and DNS server for a limited lease period. These are separate services with different jobs.
topics.importance: Unexpected DNS activity or repeated address assignment can be useful investigation clues. Analysts need to know what normal name lookups and network configuration look like.
steps: A device joins a network and requests configuration.
A DHCP service offers network settings for a lease.
The device uses a DNS resolver to look up a service name.
The resolver returns records that help the device contact the service.
topics.example: When a laptop joins a home Wi-Fi network, DHCP may provide its local address. When the learner opens a website name, DNS helps find the destination address.
topics.cyberExample: A defender may review DNS logs for unusual lookup patterns. A single unfamiliar name is not proof of harm; context and corroborating evidence are needed.

terms.meaning: A service that looks up DNS information for a client.
A time-limited assignment of network settings.
A named entry containing information such as an address or mail service.

topics.diagram: JOIN NETWORK -> DHCP PROVIDES SETTINGS -> DNS LOOKS UP NAME -> CONNECT
topics.activity: Write down the everyday steps between joining a Wi-Fi network and opening a website. Keep all examples to services you normally use.

topics.title: TCP and UDP
topics.definition: TCP and UDP are transport protocols that help applications exchange data, but they handle delivery differently.
topics.explanation: Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) establishes a connection and tracks delivery so missing data can be sent again and received in order. User Datagram Protocol (UDP) sends individual datagrams without the same delivery guarantees. Applications choose based on their needs. Neither protocol is automatically safe or unsafe; security also depends on the application, configuration, and protections around the traffic.
topics.importance: A SOC Analyst may use a protocol name to understand what type of communication a log describes and which expected behavior to compare it with.
steps: The application chooses a transport protocol.
The operating system adds transport information such as source and destination ports.
Network layers carry the data toward the destination.
The receiving application handles the data according to its protocol.
topics.example: A file transfer may use a reliable ordered connection. A live voice service may prefer fast delivery and handle a small amount of loss itself.
topics.cyberExample: A firewall record showing UDP or TCP describes transport, not intent. The destination service, time, and approved use still need review.

terms.meaning: A connection-oriented transport with delivery and ordering mechanisms.
A connectionless transport that does not provide TCP's delivery guarantees.
A self-contained unit of data sent using a protocol such as UDP.

topics.diagram: APPLICATION DATA -> TCP (tracked stream) OR UDP (datagrams) -> IP NETWORK
topics.activity: Explain in your own words why a real-time voice application may choose different transport behavior from a file download.

topics.title: Common network ports
topics.definition: A port number helps a computer deliver network traffic to the correct application or service on a device.
topics.explanation: IP addresses identify network endpoints; port numbers distinguish services using those endpoints. Common examples include 53 for DNS, 80 for HTTP, 443 for HTTPS, 22 for SSH, and 25 for SMTP. These are conventions, not guarantees: services can use other ports, and a port number alone does not reveal what a service is doing.
topics.importance: Ports are common fields in firewall, server, and network-monitoring records. Knowing a few common conventions helps an analyst read alerts without jumping to conclusions.
steps: A service listens for traffic on an address and port.
A client sends traffic to that destination.
Network controls allow or block it according to policy.
The service processes permitted requests and records relevant events.
topics.example: A browser normally uses destination port 443 for an HTTPS website connection, but the service owner can configure a different port.
topics.cyberExample: A firewall alert about an unexpected destination port should be checked against the asset's approved services and recent change records.

terms.meaning: A numbered logical endpoint used to direct traffic to an application service.
Waiting for incoming communication on a configured address or port.
A program that provides a function to other programs or users.

topics.diagram:
DEVICE ADDRESS + PORT -> NETWORK SERVICE
Example: server address + 443 -> HTTPS service (common convention)
topics.activity: Match these documented examples: DNS 53, HTTP 80, HTTPS 443. State why the number alone cannot prove which program is listening.

topics.title: HTTP and HTTPS
topics.definition: HTTP is a protocol for exchanging web requests and responses. HTTPS is HTTP carried through a protected TLS connection.
topics.explanation: A browser sends a request describing a resource and a server returns a response. Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) defines message rules. HTTPS uses Transport Layer Security (TLS) to protect the connection from reading or unnoticed changes while it travels, and to help verify the server's identity. HTTPS does not prove that a website is honest or that its content is safe.
topics.importance: SOC Analysts may review web logs and alerts. Understanding the difference between encrypted transport and trustworthy content prevents false reassurance.
steps: The browser identifies a site and requests a connection.
For HTTPS, the browser and server negotiate TLS protection and check certificates.
The browser sends an HTTP request through the protected connection.
The server returns an HTTP response through that connection.
topics.example: A browser uses HTTPS to protect a learner's connection to a course website. The protection does not guarantee that the course itself is accurate.
topics.cyberExample: A suspicious email can link to a site that uses HTTPS. Analysts should consider the sender, domain, purpose, and approved reporting process rather than trusting the lock icon alone.

terms.meaning: A request-and-response protocol used by web applications.
HTTP protected by TLS during transport.
A protocol that can provide encryption, integrity, and server authentication for a connection.
A digital statement used in checking a service's identity.

topics.diagram:
BROWSER -- TLS-PROTECTED HTTPS REQUEST --> WEB SERVER
BROWSER <-- TLS-PROTECTED HTTPS RESPONSE -- WEB SERVER
topics.activity: Inspect the address bar of a site you already trust and identify whether it uses HTTPS. Do not enter credentials on unfamiliar sites.

topics.title: Routers, switches, and firewalls
topics.definition: A switch connects devices on a local network, a router forwards traffic between networks, and a firewall applies rules to network traffic.
topics.explanation: A switch commonly delivers local traffic to the correct connected device. A router chooses a path between different networks. A firewall allows or blocks traffic according to configured rules. These roles can exist in separate devices or be combined in one product. A firewall is only as useful as its policy, maintenance, and monitoring.
topics.importance: Knowing which device performs a control helps analysts find the right logs and team when investigating a network event.
steps: A device sends traffic toward a local destination or gateway.
A switch handles delivery within its local network segment.
A router forwards traffic between network segments.
A firewall evaluates relevant traffic against policy and records allowed or blocked events when configured.
topics.example: In a small home network, one box may provide Wi-Fi, routing, and basic firewall functions. In a larger organization those duties may be split across managed devices.
topics.cyberExample: A firewall can restrict a user network from reaching server-management ports unless there is an approved need.

terms.meaning: A device that connects systems within a local network.
A device that forwards traffic between networks.
A control that permits or blocks traffic according to rules.
Separating a network into areas with controlled communication.

topics.diagram: WORKSTATIONS -> SWITCH -> FIREWALL / ROUTER -> OTHER NETWORKS
topics.activity: Draw a fictional office with a staff network, a guest network, and a server network. Mark where a firewall rule could limit unnecessary communication.

topics.title: Basic network communication
topics.definition: Network communication is the exchange of messages between applications through multiple layers of protocols and equipment.
topics.explanation: A message is prepared by an application, wrapped with transport and network details, and sent across a local link. Routers forward it toward the destination network. The destination removes the delivery information and passes the message to the right application. This layered approach lets many devices and networks work together.
topics.importance: This model gives analysts a practical way to read a network event: identify the source, destination, service, time, and outcome before proposing an explanation.
steps: The application creates a request.
Transport information identifies the communicating services.
IP information identifies source and destination endpoints.
Local network equipment delivers the message to the next hop.
The destination service responds, and logs may record the exchange.
topics.example: When a browser requests a course page, it contacts a web service, receives a response, and displays the returned content.
topics.cyberExample: A synthetic firewall record might show a test workstation connecting to a training server on a documented service port. An analyst checks whether the connection matches the lab plan.

terms.meaning: The endpoint that begins or sends a communication.
The endpoint a communication is intended to reach.
The next network device that forwards traffic on its route.

topics.diagram: APPLICATION -> TRANSPORT -> IP ADDRESSING -> LOCAL LINK -> ROUTED NETWORK -> SERVICE
topics.activity: Using a fictional example, write down the source, destination, service, and reason for one allowed training connection.

quiz.prompt: What is the main job of an IP address?
choices: Identify a destination for network routing
quiz.explanation: IP addresses help direct traffic to network endpoints; they do not prove a person's identity.

quiz.prompt: What does DHCP commonly provide to a device?
choices: Network settings such as an address and router
A guarantee that a website is safe
A permanent identity for a person
quiz.explanation: DHCP commonly leases addresses and other network settings to devices.

quiz.prompt: Which statement about HTTPS is correct?
choices: It protects transport but does not prove a site is honest
It guarantees every page is safe
It replaces the need for account security
quiz.explanation: HTTPS protects the connection, but users and analysts still need to assess the site's identity and purpose.

quiz.prompt: Which device role forwards traffic between networks?
quiz.explanation: Routers forward traffic between networks. A switch commonly connects devices on a local network.

quiz.prompt: A port number alone proves what program is running. True or false?
quiz.explanation: Port numbers are conventions; services can be configured differently, so context is required.

modules.title: Operating System Fundamentals
modules.description: Learn how Windows and Linux manage accounts, files, programs, services, and system records.

topics.title: What is an operating system?
topics.definition: An operating system is the core software that manages a computer's resources and provides a consistent way for applications and people to use them.
topics.explanation: The operating system coordinates processor time, memory, storage, devices, accounts, and network connections. It provides common services so each application does not need to control every hardware part on its own. Different operating systems make different design choices, but they all perform many of these shared jobs.
topics.importance: Security work depends on operating-system context. The same event can be stored in different places and described with different names on Windows and Linux.
steps: Startup code locates and loads the operating system.
The operating system prepares hardware and background services.
A user signs in under an account.
Applications request resources through operating-system services.
topics.example: A text editor asks the operating system to open a file, display a window, and save changes to storage.
topics.cyberExample: An analyst first identifies which operating system produced a log before applying platform-specific steps from an approved investigation guide.

terms.meaning: The central part of an operating system that manages hardware and core resources.
Software that helps the operating system communicate with a hardware device.
A shared system capability such as processor time, memory, or storage.

topics.diagram:
APPLICATIONS
     | requests
OPERATING SYSTEM (accounts, files, processes, devices)
     | controls
HARDWARE
topics.activity: Find the operating-system name and version using the normal settings interface on a device you are allowed to use.

topics.title: Windows fundamentals
topics.definition: Windows is a family of operating systems used on personal computers and servers.
topics.explanation: Windows provides a desktop, file manager, settings, user accounts, applications, and administrative tools. Common Windows concepts include drive letters, folders, services that run in the background, and Event Viewer records. A graphical interface and command-line tools can both manage the same system, but each should be used with appropriate permissions.
topics.importance: Many organizations use Windows endpoints. A SOC Analyst may need to identify the device, account, process, and Windows event records associated with an alert.
steps: A user signs in to a Windows account.
Windows loads the user's desktop and permitted settings.
Applications and background services run as processes.
Windows components and applications may write events to system logs.
topics.example: A learner can use File Explorer to find a document and Settings to check the device's update status.
topics.cyberExample: A Windows sign-in event can show whether an account sign-in succeeded or failed. Analysts use the event details and related records rather than relying on a single line alone.

terms.meaning: The Windows application used to browse files and folders.
A program that can run in the background to provide a system function.
A Windows tool for viewing records from system and application logs.

topics.diagram:
WINDOWS USER -> DESKTOP / APPLICATIONS -> WINDOWS SERVICES
                                     -> EVENT LOGS
topics.activity: Open Windows Settings or the system information page and record the edition name and version for your own notes.

topics.title: Linux fundamentals
topics.definition: Linux is an open-source operating-system kernel used in many distributions for desktops, servers, cloud systems, and embedded devices.
topics.explanation: A Linux distribution combines the Linux kernel with system tools, applications, and a package-management method. Distributions may look different, but many share concepts such as users, directories, processes, permissions, and text-based configuration. The command line is common but is not the only way to use Linux.
topics.importance: SOC Analysts may investigate Linux servers and services. Basic familiarity helps them understand account records, process lists, file ownership, and system logs.
steps: A distribution starts the Linux kernel and system services.
A user signs in through a graphical session or terminal.
Commands or applications ask the system to perform allowed tasks.
The system records selected events in logs.
topics.example: A learner can use a graphical file manager or the read-only command `pwd` to see the current working directory.
topics.cyberExample: A Linux authentication log may record sign-in events. Analysts should protect log access and follow approved procedures when reviewing them.

terms.meaning: The core of the Linux operating system that manages resources and devices.
A packaged operating system built around the Linux kernel and associated software.
A text interface used to enter commands and view output.

topics.diagram: LINUX DISTRIBUTION = LINUX KERNEL + SYSTEM TOOLS + APPLICATIONS
topics.activity: If you have an authorized Linux practice machine, run `pwd` to display the current directory. Do not run commands copied from untrusted sources.

topics.title: Users and permissions
topics.definition: A user account represents an identity on a system, and permissions describe which actions that identity may perform.
topics.explanation: Systems use accounts to associate activity with a person or service. Permissions can control who may read, change, or run information. Administrative accounts have broader powers and should be used only when needed. The least-privilege principle means giving each account only the access required for its task.
topics.importance: Excessive permissions can make mistakes or account misuse more damaging. Analysts check which identity acted and whether its access was expected.
steps: A person or service signs in with an account.
The system identifies the account and its groups or roles.
A requested action is checked against permissions.
The system allows or denies the action and may record the result.
topics.example: A shared classroom computer can give a learner permission to use a word processor without permission to change system-wide settings.
topics.cyberExample: A service account that only reads one application directory has less potential impact than one with full administrator rights.

terms.meaning: A named identity used to access a system.
A collection of accounts managed together for access decisions.
Giving an identity only the access needed for its approved work.
An account or role with broad system-management permissions.

topics.diagram: ACCOUNT + GROUPS + REQUESTED ACTION -> PERMISSION CHECK -> ALLOW OR DENY
topics.activity: Review a fictional role list and identify which account needs administrator access and which can use a standard account.

topics.title: Files and directories
topics.definition: A file stores named information, and a directory (also called a folder) organizes files and other directories.
topics.explanation: Operating systems arrange storage as a hierarchy. A path names the route to a file or directory. Windows commonly uses drive letters and backslashes in paths; Linux commonly starts paths at `/` and uses forward slashes. Permissions can apply to files and directories. A path is useful evidence but does not by itself explain why a file exists.
topics.importance: Investigators use paths to describe where a record or program was found. Accurate paths help another analyst reproduce a review without guessing.
steps: A user or program requests a path.
The system checks each directory in the path.
Permissions are checked for the requested action.
The file is opened, changed, or denied according to policy.
topics.example: A Windows path might be `C:\Users\Student\Documents\notes.txt`. A Linux path might be `/home/student/notes.txt`.
topics.cyberExample: A file in an unexpected location may deserve review, but its location alone does not prove it is harmful. Check ownership, timestamp, purpose, and related events.

terms.meaning: A container used to organize files and other directories.
A full path beginning from a system's root or drive.
The account associated with a file or directory for management and access checks.

topics.diagram:
ROOT
  +-- users
      +-- learner
          +-- documents
              +-- notes.txt
topics.activity: Use a file manager to view the path of a practice document. Do not inspect private files or change permissions.

topics.title: Processes and services
topics.definition: A process is a running program, and a service is a program designed to provide a background function.
topics.explanation: When a program starts, the operating system creates a process with its own running state and resource use. A service may start automatically and work without a visible window, such as a time-sync or update service. A system can have many expected processes. An unfamiliar name needs context before an analyst decides it is unusual.
topics.importance: Process and service records help SOC Analysts connect an alert to the software that was running and the account that started it.
steps: A user or system event requests a program.
The operating system creates a process.
The process uses permitted memory, files, and network connections.
The process ends or continues as a background service.
topics.example: A clock application may run briefly to show the time, while a print service waits in the background for print jobs.
topics.cyberExample: A process using an unusual amount of resources may be investigated. Analysts record its name, owner, start time, and context before taking action.

terms.meaning: An active instance of a program.
A background program that provides an ongoing function.
Processor, memory, storage, or network activity used by a process.

topics.diagram:
START REQUEST -> PROCESS RUNS -> USES RESOURCES -> STOPS
                         +-> may provide a background service
topics.activity: Open your system's normal task or process viewer and identify one familiar application. Do not stop or change any process.

topics.title: System logs
topics.definition: A system log is a time-ordered record of events reported by an operating system, application, or service.
topics.explanation: Logs can record sign-ins, updates, errors, service changes, and other events. A log entry may include a time, event type, account, device, and result. Systems do not record everything, and clocks or settings can affect records. Logs should be protected from unauthorized changes and interpreted with related evidence.
topics.importance: Logs are a core source of evidence for monitoring and investigations. Good analysis distinguishes what a record directly says from what an analyst infers.
steps: A system component experiences an event.
Logging settings determine whether and how the event is recorded.
The record is stored locally or sent to a monitoring service.
An analyst searches, correlates, and documents relevant entries.
topics.example: An application may record that it started successfully at a certain time and under a particular service account.
topics.cyberExample: A failed sign-in followed by a successful sign-in may need review. The analyst checks account, source device, normal schedule, and related events before deciding whether it is suspicious.

terms.meaning: A date and time associated with a record.
The system component or application that created a log entry.
Comparing related records to understand a sequence of events.

topics.diagram: EVENT -> LOG SOURCE -> STORED RECORDS -> SEARCH AND CORRELATION -> INVESTIGATION NOTE
topics.activity: Read the fictional record `10:14 account=learner result=failed`. Write only what it states and list two facts you would need before interpreting it.

topics.title: Basic command-line use
topics.definition: A command line is a text interface where a person enters commands and reads system output.
topics.explanation: Commands can be useful for repeatable system tasks. A command has a name and may have options or arguments. Different operating systems use different command interpreters and syntax. Read output carefully and understand a command before running it; some commands can change or delete data.
topics.importance: Analysts often use command-line tools to inspect a system efficiently. Safe, read-only commands are a good starting point for beginners.
steps: Open a terminal approved for practice.
Read the prompt and confirm which system or account you are using.
Enter one understood, read-only command.
Review the output and close the terminal when finished.
topics.example: On Linux, `whoami` displays the current account and `pwd` displays the current directory. In PowerShell, `Get-Location` displays the current location.
topics.cyberExample: An analyst may use an approved read-only command to identify a system or inspect a process list. Do not run commands from an alert or website without understanding their effect and authorization.

terms.meaning: A program that reads commands and communicates with the operating system.
Additional information supplied to a command.
An operation that observes information without intentionally changing it.

topics.diagram: PERSON -> COMMAND LINE -> SHELL CHECKS COMMAND -> OPERATING SYSTEM -> OUTPUT
topics.activity: In an authorized practice environment, run only `whoami` or `Get-Location` and write down what the output means. Do not use administrator privileges.

quiz.prompt: What is the operating system's main role?
choices: Manage resources and provide services to applications
quiz.explanation: The operating system manages hardware, accounts, files, processes, and shared services.

quiz.prompt: What does least privilege mean?
choices: Give each account only the access needed for approved work
quiz.explanation: Least privilege limits access to what is needed for an approved task.

quiz.prompt: What is a process?
choices: A running instance of a program
quiz.explanation: A process is an active program instance managed by the operating system.

quiz.prompt: A single unusual log entry proves an account was compromised. True or false?
choices: Only if it has a timestamp
quiz.explanation: A log entry is evidence to investigate. Context and related records are needed before drawing a conclusion.

quiz.prompt: What is the safest way to learn command-line tools?
choices: Run commands you understand in an authorized practice environment
Copy commands from unknown websites as administrator
Try commands on a work server without permission
quiz.explanation: Use only understood, authorized, preferably read-only commands in a safe practice environment.

modules.title: Linux Fundamentals
modules.description: Learn Linux systems, files, safe terminal use, permissions, processes, networking, and security basics.

topics.title: Introduction to Linux
topics.definition: Linux is a family of operating systems built around the Linux kernel.
topics.explanation: The kernel coordinates hardware, memory, processes, files, and devices. Other tools provide a shell, graphical desktop, package manager, and applications. Linux powers servers, cloud systems, phones, embedded devices, and analyst workstations.
topics.importance: SOC Analysts often examine Linux servers and logs, so recognizing its basic tools and conventions helps them investigate accurately.
steps: A computer starts its boot firmware.
The bootloader loads a Linux kernel.
The kernel starts system services and presents a shell or desktop.
Users and applications request managed resources.
topics.example: A library server can run Linux to host its catalog around the clock with controlled user accounts.
topics.cyberExample: An analyst may review a Linux authentication log to confirm whether an approved account signed in at a particular time.

terms.meaning: The operating-system core that manages hardware and system resources.
A command interface that lets a user request operating-system tasks.

topics.diagram: POWER ON -> BOOTLOADER -> LINUX KERNEL -> SERVICES -> USER PROGRAMS
topics.activity: On a device you own or an approved virtual machine, identify whether its operating system is Linux; do not change system settings.
topics.demonstration: In a Linux terminal, run uname -s. Expected output: Linux. This only displays the kernel name.
topics.mistakes: Linux is not one single desktop product, and the shell is not the kernel; they are separate layers.
topics.summary: Linux combines a kernel with tools and applications to make a complete operating system.

topics.title: What is a Linux distribution?
topics.definition: A Linux distribution packages the kernel with selected tools, applications, defaults, and update services.
topics.explanation: Maintainers choose a release model, software repositories, installer, desktop options, and support period. A package manager downloads signed packages from configured repositories. The distribution provides a consistent way to install updates and manage dependencies.
topics.importance: Distribution details affect command availability, package names, update procedures, and where an analyst expects configuration or log files.
steps: A project selects a kernel and software versions.
Maintainers assemble defaults and trusted repositories.
Users install the distribution on a computer or virtual machine.
Updates arrive through its documented package process.
topics.example: Two schools may use different distributions while running the same web browser and office tools.
topics.cyberExample: Before applying an update during incident response, an analyst identifies the distribution and follows its approved patch process.

terms.meaning: A packaged Linux operating system with its own tools and policies.
A configured source of software packages and updates.

topics.diagram: KERNEL + SYSTEM TOOLS + PACKAGE SOURCES + DEFAULTS = DISTRIBUTION
topics.activity: Read the distribution name in the settings or release information of an authorized Linux practice machine.
topics.demonstration: On many distributions, cat /etc/os-release prints the distribution name and version; read it only.
topics.mistakes: Do not assume package commands or support dates are identical across distributions.
topics.summary: A distribution makes Linux usable by selecting, integrating, and maintaining its software.

topics.title: Popular Linux distributions
topics.definition: Linux distributions serve different needs, from stable servers to learning desktops and embedded devices.
topics.explanation: Debian and Ubuntu emphasize broad use and repositories; Red Hat Enterprise Linux and compatible systems focus on managed enterprise support; Fedora offers newer community releases. Alpine targets compact environments. Each has a distinct lifecycle and package ecosystem.
topics.importance: Knowing the family helps a defender read documentation and avoid applying commands or update advice to the wrong system.
steps: Identify the distribution and release.
Check its official support lifecycle.
Use its package manager and vendor guidance.
Record the exact version when documenting an issue.
topics.example: A developer may use Ubuntu on a laptop while a company uses an enterprise Linux release on production servers.
topics.cyberExample: An alert mentioning a package version must be compared with the relevant distribution's security advisory, not a random version list.

terms.meaning: A long-term-support release maintained for a published period.
The supported period during which a release receives maintenance.

topics.diagram:
DEBIAN FAMILY: apt   |   RED HAT FAMILY: dnf   |   ALPINE: apk
Always confirm the installed distribution before following instructions.
topics.activity: Compare the published support pages for two distributions without installing software; note how each describes updates.
topics.demonstration: Use cat /etc/os-release to identify a practice system, then consult only that distribution's official documentation.
topics.mistakes: A familiar distribution name does not prove that a particular release is still supported.
topics.summary: Choose tools and security guidance that match the actual distribution and version.

topics.title: Linux architecture
topics.definition: Linux architecture describes how hardware, the kernel, system services, shells, and applications work together.
topics.explanation: The kernel handles low-level operations. System libraries expose common functions; services run background tasks; shells and desktops accept user actions. Applications request resources through these layers instead of controlling hardware directly.
topics.importance: This layered view helps an analyst locate whether a symptom belongs to an application, a service, permissions, or the operating system.
steps: A user starts an application.
The application requests a system function through libraries.
The kernel checks and performs permitted resource work.
The application displays or records the result.
topics.example: A music player asks system services to read an audio file and send sound to speakers.
topics.cyberExample: A service account running a web service should have only the permissions that service requires.

terms.meaning: A background program that provides a system or network function.
Reusable software functions that applications call to request common work.

topics.diagram: USER -> SHELL / DESKTOP -> APPLICATION -> LIBRARIES -> KERNEL -> HARDWARE
topics.activity: Draw the layer an application uses when opening a local document, then note where access permissions are checked.
topics.demonstration: Run ps -p 1 -o comm= on a Linux practice system to read the name of the first process; output varies by distribution.
topics.mistakes: A service is a program, not the same thing as the kernel or the physical computer.
topics.summary: Linux layers separate user-facing programs from managed system resources.

topics.title: Linux file system structure
topics.definition: Linux organizes files under one directory tree that begins at the root directory, written as slash.
topics.explanation: Paths such as /home/learner and /var/log describe locations in that tree. Common directories have conventions: /etc for configuration, /var/log for many logs, /home for user files, and /tmp for temporary files. Actual layouts can vary.
topics.importance: Knowing common locations helps analysts find configuration and logs without searching blindly or changing unrelated files.
steps: Start from the root directory /.
Follow each directory name in a path.
Check permissions before reading or changing an item.
Use the distribution's documentation for system-specific locations.
topics.example: A person's work notes may live under /home/learner/Documents.
topics.cyberExample: An analyst reads an approved log under /var/log to establish a timeline, preserving the original evidence.

terms.meaning: The top of the Linux directory tree, written as /.
A complete location beginning at the root directory.

topics.diagram: / -> etc/ (configuration)   home/ (users)   var/log/ (logs)   tmp/ (temporary)
topics.activity: Use ls to inspect your own home directory and identify folders; do not open unfamiliar files.
topics.demonstration: The path /var/log/auth.log is used on some systems; others use /var/log/secure or a journal. Check local documentation.
topics.mistakes: Do not assume every distribution stores a particular log at the same path.
topics.summary: Linux paths form one tree, with familiar directories used for common purposes.

topics.title: Files and directories
topics.definition: A file stores named data, while a directory organizes names of files and other directories.
topics.explanation: Names can include extensions, but extensions are hints rather than proof of file contents. Linux paths distinguish uppercase from lowercase. A relative path starts from the current directory; an absolute path starts from /.
topics.importance: Analysts use file paths and metadata to describe evidence precisely and avoid confusing similarly named files.
steps: Choose a directory you are allowed to use.
Create or locate an item by its exact path.
Check its name and permissions.
Record the full path when reporting a finding.
topics.example: Notes.txt and notes.txt can be two different Linux filenames.
topics.cyberExample: A suspicious filename alone does not establish that a file is malicious; analysts verify source and context using approved tools.

terms.meaning: A container used to organize filesystem entries.
A location interpreted from the current working directory.

topics.diagram:
/home/learner/ -> Documents/ -> notes.txt
           absolute path; each slash separates a directory name
topics.activity: In a personal practice folder, create a text file and record its full path with pwd and ls.
topics.demonstration: Run pwd, then ls. The first prints the current location; the second lists visible entries there.
topics.mistakes: Linux filenames are case-sensitive, and an extension does not guarantee a file's true format.
topics.summary: Use exact paths and names to navigate and describe Linux files.

topics.title: Basic Linux commands
topics.definition: A Linux command is an instruction entered into a shell, often with options and arguments.
topics.explanation: The shell interprets the command and asks the operating system to perform it. Spaces separate arguments; options usually adjust behavior. Output and exit status help indicate what happened. Read help pages before using unfamiliar commands.
topics.importance: Command-line fluency lets analysts inspect systems consistently, but a mistaken command can alter or remove data.
steps: Confirm the authorized machine and current account.
Read the command's help or manual page.
Prefer inspection commands while learning.
Review output and report errors rather than guessing.
topics.example: The date command displays the system's current date and time.
topics.cyberExample: An approved analyst may use a read-only command to collect system context before escalating an alert.

terms.meaning: A command setting that changes how a command behaves.
A numeric result that commonly indicates success or failure.

topics.diagram: PROMPT + COMMAND + OPTIONS / ARGUMENTS -> SHELL -> OUTPUT
topics.activity: Run date and whoami in an authorized practice terminal, then explain each output in one sentence.
topics.demonstration:
$ whoami
learner
$ date
Output is the practice system's current local date and time.
topics.mistakes: Do not paste commands from untrusted sources or add administrator privileges just to suppress an error.
topics.summary: Understand a command's effect and context before running it.

topics.title: Navigation commands: pwd, ls and cd
topics.definition: pwd prints the current directory, ls lists entries, and cd changes the shell's current directory.
topics.explanation: Together these commands help users orient themselves before file work. Options can change listing details. Use quotes or escape spaces in paths, and verify the destination before running commands that change files.
topics.importance: Knowing the current path prevents accidental actions in the wrong directory and makes investigation notes reproducible.
steps: Run pwd to confirm the starting location.
Use ls to view available names.
Use cd with a known directory path.
Run pwd again to verify the change.
topics.example: A learner changes from their home directory into Documents to find a class note.
topics.cyberExample: Before examining an exported log, an analyst confirms they are in the approved evidence folder.

terms.meaning: The directory a shell uses as the starting point for relative paths.
A user's personal starting directory, often /home/name.

topics.diagram: pwd -> confirm location | ls -> inspect names | cd path -> move | pwd -> verify
topics.activity: Use pwd, ls, and cd only within your own practice folder; return to the folder where you began.
topics.demonstration:
$ pwd
/home/learner
$ cd Documents
$ pwd
/home/learner/Documents
topics.mistakes: Running cd changes the shell location, not the location of files; relative paths depend on that current location.
topics.summary: Check where you are before and after navigating.

topics.title: File management commands: touch, mkdir, cp, mv and rm
topics.definition: These commands create, copy, move, rename, or remove files and directories.
topics.explanation: touch creates an empty file or updates a timestamp; mkdir creates a directory; cp copies; mv moves or renames; rm removes. These commands can change data, so use only a clearly named practice folder and verify paths first.
topics.importance: Analysts need to collect and organize files carefully while preserving evidence and avoiding accidental loss.
steps: Create a practice directory with mkdir.
Create a harmless note with touch.
Copy it and verify both names with ls.
Remove only your temporary copy after checking its exact path.
topics.example: A student copies a draft before editing so the original remains available.
topics.cyberExample: During an investigation, preserve original evidence and work from an authorized copy according to policy.

terms.meaning: A second file containing copied data.
Changing an item's directory or name.
Deleting a file entry; recovery may not be possible.

topics.diagram: mkdir practice -> touch note -> cp note copy -> mv copy renamed -> rm renamed
topics.activity: Use only the commands shown in the demonstration, inside a new personal directory; verify every target before removal.
topics.demonstration:
$ mkdir -p ~/cyberpath-practice
$ cd ~/cyberpath-practice
$ touch note.txt
$ cp note.txt note-copy.txt
$ ls
note-copy.txt  note.txt
$ mv note-copy.txt renamed.txt
$ ls
note.txt  renamed.txt
$ rm -i renamed.txt
rm: remove regular empty file 'renamed.txt'? y
topics.mistakes: Never practice rm with wildcards, administrator privileges, or system paths; a typo can delete important data.
topics.summary: File commands are useful but potentially destructive; isolate practice and verify exact paths.

topics.title: Reading files: cat, less and head
topics.definition: cat, less, and head display file contents in different ways without editing the file.
topics.explanation: cat is convenient for short files, less lets a reader page through long files, and head displays the first lines. Use a known text file and avoid printing sensitive content to a shared screen or transcript.
topics.importance: Log reading begins with careful observation; choosing a suitable viewer makes long records easier to inspect.
steps: Confirm the file path and authorization.
Use head for a quick preview or less for long content.
Search and navigate carefully in the viewer.
Exit less with q and record only relevant facts.
topics.example: A learner reads the first few lines of a class notes file before opening the full document.
topics.cyberExample: An analyst reviews a permitted sample log without changing its original contents.

terms.meaning: The normal text output area where a command displays results.
A program that lets users read output one screen at a time.

topics.diagram: SHORT FILE -> cat | FIRST LINES -> head | LONG FILE -> less
topics.activity: Create a few harmless lines in a practice text file, then compare head and less.
topics.demonstration:
$ printf 'alpha\nbeta\ngamma\n' > sample.txt
$ head -n 2 sample.txt
alpha
beta
$ cat sample.txt
alpha
beta
gamma
topics.mistakes: cat is not ideal for huge files, and displaying sensitive logs may expose data to bystanders.
topics.summary: Choose a read-only viewer suited to the file size and sensitivity.

topics.title: File permissions
topics.definition: Linux permissions specify which users may read, write, or execute a file or directory.
topics.explanation: Permissions are expressed for the owner, group, and other users. For files, read views content, write changes it, and execute runs it. For directories, permissions affect listing, creating, and entering; ownership and access-control rules can add detail.
topics.importance: Correct permissions reduce accidental exposure and restrict what an account or service can change.
steps: Identify the file owner and group.
Read the permission bits.
Compare access with the task's need.
Ask an administrator to correct overbroad access.
topics.example: A shared class handout may be readable by a group while only its owner can edit it.
topics.cyberExample: A service should not be able to read private user files unless its job requires that access.

terms.meaning: Permission to view a file's contents or list a directory.
Permission to change a file or create entries in a directory.
Permission to run a file or traverse a directory.

topics.diagram:
OWNER | GROUP | OTHERS
  rwx  |  r-x  |  ---
r=read, w=write, x=execute
topics.activity: Use ls -l on a practice file and explain its owner, group, and permission characters without changing them.
topics.demonstration:
$ ls -l sample.txt
-rw-r--r-- 1 learner learners 18 sample.txt
Owner can read/write; group and others can read.
topics.mistakes: The execute bit has different practical meaning on a file and on a directory.
topics.summary: Permissions express access for owners, groups, and other users.

topics.title: chmod and chown
topics.definition: chmod changes permission bits, while chown changes the owner or group of a filesystem item.
topics.explanation: Symbolic and numeric modes can describe permissions; chown often requires administrative authority. Changes should be narrowly scoped, approved, and verified. Never recursively change permissions or ownership on system directories as a learning exercise.
topics.importance: Incorrect changes can expose sensitive files or break services, while least-privilege corrections can reduce risk.
steps: Inspect the existing owner and permissions.
Confirm the approved account and required access.
Apply the smallest authorized change to a practice item.
Recheck the result and document it.
topics.example: A personal script may need execute permission for its owner but not for every user.
topics.cyberExample: An administrator restricts a confidential configuration file to the service account and approved administrators.

terms.meaning: Command for changing filesystem permission bits.
Command for changing file ownership or group.

topics.diagram: inspect ls -l -> confirm need -> narrow authorized change -> verify ls -l
topics.activity: On a disposable practice file, inspect chmod documentation and describe what a proposed mode would permit; do not alter system files.
topics.demonstration:
$ chmod u+x practice-script.sh
$ ls -l practice-script.sh
The owner's execute bit is added; use only on your own practice file.
topics.mistakes: Avoid broad modes such as granting write access to everyone and never use sudo casually.
topics.summary: Change ownership and permissions only when authorized and only as broadly as required.

topics.title: Users and groups
topics.definition: Users identify accounts, while groups let administrators assign shared access to selected accounts.
topics.explanation: Linux system files and services commonly run under dedicated identities. Group membership can grant access to shared resources. Administrators should review memberships and disable unused accounts through approved procedures.
topics.importance: Account and group records help analysts understand who could access a file or service at a given time.
steps: Identify the account involved in an event.
Check its approved role and group membership.
Compare access with job requirements.
Report unexpected access for authorized review.
topics.example: A project group lets several teammates read shared documents without sharing one password.
topics.cyberExample: A service runs under a dedicated low-privilege account rather than a human administrator account.

terms.meaning: Numeric identifier associated with a Linux user account.
Numeric identifier associated with a Linux group.

topics.diagram: USER ACCOUNT -> GROUP MEMBERSHIP -> PERMITTED SHARED RESOURCE
topics.activity: Run id in an authorized practice account and identify the current username and groups shown.
topics.demonstration:
$ id
uid=1000(learner) gid=1000(learner) groups=1000(learner)
topics.mistakes: A shared group does not mean all members should receive administrator privileges.
topics.summary: Use named accounts and narrowly scoped groups to manage access.

topics.title: Process management
topics.definition: A process is a running program with an identifier and an execution context managed by Linux.
topics.explanation: The operating system schedules processes and tracks their resource use. Read-only tools can list processes and owners. Stopping a process changes system state and can disrupt users, so it requires authorization and impact assessment.
topics.importance: Process context helps analysts distinguish expected services from unusual activity without treating a name alone as proof.
steps: List processes with an approved inspection tool.
Note the process ID, owner, command, and time.
Compare with system purpose and baseline.
Escalate suspicious findings before taking action.
topics.example: A text editor process appears while a person is editing a document.
topics.cyberExample: An analyst correlates an unexpected service process with its account, parent process, and change record.

terms.meaning: Process identifier assigned by the operating system.
The process that started another process.

topics.diagram: USER ACTION -> PARENT PROCESS -> CHILD PROCESS -> RESOURCE USE
topics.activity: Use ps to list processes on your practice machine and identify one familiar application; do not terminate processes.
topics.demonstration:
$ ps -eo pid,user,comm --sort=pid | head
PID USER COMMAND
  1 root systemd
Output varies; this read-only listing does not stop processes.
topics.mistakes: An unfamiliar process name alone is not proof of malware, and killing a process can destroy useful evidence.
topics.summary: Inspect process ownership and relationships before drawing conclusions or intervening.

topics.title: Linux networking commands
topics.definition: Linux networking commands inspect local interfaces, routes, name resolution, and connection state.
topics.explanation: ip addr shows interface addresses, ip route shows routing choices, and ss can list sockets. These commands observe local configuration. Network testing should remain within an authorized lab or a local address.
topics.importance: A defender needs basic network context to interpret logs and determine which interface or route a system uses.
steps: Confirm the system and authorization.
Inspect local addresses and routes.
Record the time and relevant interface.
Avoid probing systems outside the approved scope.
topics.example: A support technician checks whether a laptop has joined the expected office network.
topics.cyberExample: An analyst compares a server's local address with the source and destination fields in a firewall record.

terms.meaning: A network connection point, physical or virtual.
A rule that selects where network traffic is sent.

topics.diagram: APPLICATION -> NETWORK INTERFACE -> ROUTE -> APPROVED NETWORK
topics.activity: In an authorized practice environment, inspect only your machine's own interface and route information.
topics.demonstration:
$ ip addr
$ ip route
$ ss -tuln
These commands display local interface, route, and listening-socket information.
topics.mistakes: A listening socket is not automatically exposed to the internet; verify interface, firewall, and network context.
topics.summary: Read local network configuration first and keep checks within authorized scope.

topics.title: Linux log files
topics.definition: Linux logs record system, application, authentication, and service events for later review.
topics.explanation: Many systems use systemd journal; others write files under /var/log. Access may be restricted because logs can contain personal or sensitive operational data. Time zones, retention, and rotation affect interpretation.
topics.importance: Logs help reconstruct events, but a missing entry may reflect retention or configuration rather than proof nothing happened.
steps: Confirm authorization and the relevant host.
Identify the logging service and time zone.
Read only the necessary records.
Preserve the source and document filters used.
topics.example: A service owner checks recent startup messages after an approved maintenance window.
topics.cyberExample: An analyst compares authentication events with a ticketed maintenance activity before escalating.

terms.meaning: A structured collection of system event records, such as systemd-journald.
Archiving or replacing older log files to manage storage.

topics.diagram: SERVICE / KERNEL -> LOGGING SERVICE -> JOURNAL OR FILE -> AUTHORIZED REVIEW
topics.activity: Read a provided fictional log sample and note its timestamp, account, event, and uncertainty.
topics.demonstration:
journalctl -n 5 --no-pager
Displays the five latest journal entries where permissions allow; review only authorized systems.
topics.mistakes: Do not assume all distributions use the same authentication log filename or time zone.
topics.summary: Treat logs as sensitive evidence and interpret them with source and time context.

topics.title: Basic Linux security practices
topics.definition: Linux security uses updates, least privilege, strong identity controls, backups, and monitoring to reduce risk.
topics.explanation: Administrators maintain supported releases, install updates through approved channels, remove unneeded services, protect credentials, and review access. Backups should be tested. Changes are planned and documented rather than improvised during a suspected incident.
topics.importance: Layered defensive controls reduce the chance that one mistake or vulnerability becomes a major disruption.
steps: Inventory systems and owners.
Apply approved updates and configuration baselines.
Limit accounts and service permissions.
Monitor logs and test recoverable backups.
topics.example: A small office schedules updates and checks that its backups can be restored.
topics.cyberExample: A server exposes only required services and uses individual accounts with monitored administrative access.

terms.meaning: Giving an identity only the access needed for approved work.
An approved reference configuration used to identify changes.

topics.diagram: PATCH + LEAST PRIVILEGE + MINIMAL SERVICES + BACKUPS + MONITORING
topics.activity: Review a public hardening checklist from the vendor for a practice distribution; do not apply changes to production.
topics.demonstration: A safe review starts with version and update status checks; actual installation belongs to an authorized change window.
topics.mistakes: Security is not achieved by copying a hardening command without understanding its impact or recovery plan.
topics.summary: Secure Linux through maintained software, controlled access, minimal exposure, and tested recovery.

quiz.prompt: What is a Linux distribution?
choices: A packaged operating system with selected tools and update sources
A single command that lists files
quiz.explanation: A distribution combines the Linux kernel with software, defaults, and maintenance choices.

quiz.prompt: Which command confirms the current working directory?
quiz.explanation: pwd prints the current directory path.

quiz.prompt: What is the safest way to practice file-removal commands?
choices: Use a disposable personal practice directory and verify the exact target
Use wildcards as administrator in system directories
quiz.explanation: File removal can be irreversible, so practice only on known temporary files in an authorized location.

quiz.prompt: What does least privilege mean?
choices: Grant only the access needed for approved work
quiz.explanation: Least privilege limits each identity's access to the minimum needed.

quiz.prompt: Does one unfamiliar process name prove a system is compromised?
choices: No; review ownership, context, and related evidence
quiz.explanation: Process names alone are not proof; analysts corroborate with context and other records.

modules.title: Cybersecurity Fundamentals
modules.description: Understand security goals, threats and risk, common attack patterns, identity controls, encryption, and practical defenses.

topics.title: Introduction to cybersecurity
topics.definition: Cybersecurity protects systems, accounts, networks, and information from misuse, damage, and disruption.
